A new type of recurrent neural network unit, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), has been developed by combining Legendre polynomial mathematics and neural network concepts. By encoding sequential information and leveraging polynomial properties, the LMU excels in capturing long-term dependencies while offering an efficient architecture with reduced computational complexity and parameters. Comparative evaluations demonstrate that the LMU outperforms the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model and rivals the performance of the transformer model in forecasting time series data. Furthermore, our findings highlight the effectiveness of the LMU in handling long-term dependencies while maintaining a parameter-efficient design that surpasses both LSTM and transformer models.

Recent experiments have shown significant interest in feebly interacting particles beyond the Standard Model. These particles are relevant not only to understanding dark matter but also to particle physics. Despite multiple theoretical models for such particles, there is a lack of established methods for identifying them. This paper proposes a universal, phenomenological approach to studying these particles by associating them with matrix elements of physical processes. This study will demonstrate how applications of sum rules can reveal the properties of these particles and ultimately enable the detection of their existence and characteristics.

Language is a type of information that can be spread through communication. We investigate and compare the effects of a finite population exchanging information through messages and migrating, focusing on the formation of distinct language areas in both scenarios and under different levels of migration. Our research reveals that monolingual island formation occurs more frequently and with higher probabilities when language is transmitted through messages rather by migration. We find that the level of communication required to cause monolingual island formation in messages is more than ten times lower than the level of migration required to cause them in migration. We speculate and outline a plan to bridge the gap between our findings that are observed in the case of messages and those which are observed in migration by adapting the techniques which are used to describe the migration to the case of messages.

PINN methods have shown effectiveness in solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDE) but are plagued by the curse of dimensionality in terms of computational efficiency. We demonstrate through examples that using Fourier features in PINN can lead to converged solutions with fewer parameters, even with rapidly varying high-frequency features. However, this results in severely limited scalability due to the necessity of using wide networks. We propose a novel training approach that combines PINN with k-means clustering of training points to mitigate the efficiency issue. We show experimentally that this new method significantly outperforms using a single large kernel of Fourier features. Furthermore, we highlight the effectiveness of our method in solving high-dimensional PDEs under highly oscillatory features, multi-scale features, and complex structural patterns, particularly in scenarios that traditionally pose significant challenges.

We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), where one wave undergoes Kelvin-Voigt damping while the other undergoes Coulomb damping. This combination of damping mechanisms and the presence of the two waves make studying this system unique. Our main discovery shows that the system's energy decreases at a polynomial rate. Interestingly, this rate can be arbitrarily slow. This result significantly expands the knowledge about systems with polynomial damping. Previous studies had shown that with only Kelvin-Voigt damping, the system's energy could decay at most at a polynomial rate but the specific rate wasn't determinable without additional conditions.

To address several key limitations of deep reinforcement learning, we've made two key modifications to the standard algorithm. First, we've combined with the Case-Control method to reduce positive and negative sample imbalance. Second, we've learned value functions solely from observed positive samples. The outcome of these advancements is a new deep reinforcement learning framework called PositRL. Experimental data, specifically from open-domain dialogue tasks, demonstrates that PositRL significantly outperforms its conventional algorithmic counterparts.

We've developed an all-optical technique to produce optical nonreciprocity in a specific way: by utilizing a strongly quantum-squeezed driving beam, we create a cyclic phase shift between forward and backward propagation through a nonlinear resonator. This method achieves optical nonreciprocity without relying on the limitations of traditional isolator methods. Notably, this specific type of optical nonreciprocity can only be realized with quantum-squeezed input; classical inputs would only produce equal cyclic phase shifts in both directions. We've demonstrated that this specific type of optical nonreciprocity can be realized with specific resonator parameters.

This study examines the properties of a kernel convolution function with a concave kernel in $p$-norm. We demonstrate the existence of just one local maximum on this function without needing to assume the kernel is symmetric or unimodal. We also provide a mathematical analysis of the kernel's derivative, showing its relationship with a $q$-norm derived differential kernel. Building on this discovery, we establish the existence of an optimal, universally applicable kernel in $p$-norm by introducing a quasinormal kernel. We prove that this kernel produces a function with only one local maximum for any kernel with a concave shape. We then demonstrate the broad utility of the kernel convolution function's characteristics in solving related problems. We verify the existence of just one optimal solution in the problem of maximizing kernel convolution with a $p$-norm distance measure, thereby extending previously discovered properties. We examine an experiment comparing the effectiveness of kernel functions in different norms and present preliminary results.

The CRESST experiment, which uses superconducting gravimeters, has the capability to study dark matter particles in a broad mass range by analyzing photon emissions from Ge isotopes. By utilizing another set of Ge sources, it can also precisely determine low-mass calibration particles with minimal uncertainty in their mass. The experiment's capability to effectively separate signal from noise at the level of individual events enables efficient utilization of its full data set for dark matter searches. In this investigation, we present the results from using 51 days of taking live time with live time from an earlier investigation.

Blind image deblurring aims to sharpen a blurred picture, but traditional approaches relying on handcrafted kernels struggle to produce satisfactory outcomes due to the limitations of single-kernel use. To overcome this issue, we introduce a novel deblurring method employing a kernel mixture that automatically adjusts its adaptability based on the picture's requirements. This new structure is then incorporated into three widely utilized image deblurring models. Experimental outcomes on established benchmarks and a vast dataset of real-world images significantly outperform existing methods, while an in-depth content analysis of the adjusted kernels significantly improve upon previous results. This paper introduces a new concept, namely the associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with biweight, demonstrating its connection to a double curved Rota-Baxter system and a Rota-Baxter system with biweight under certain conditions. Furthermore, corresponding dual BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair concepts are defined, illustrating their interrelations and presenting a concrete example to illustrate the theoretical findings.

Formal verification methods like static analysis aid software developers in creating dependable systems by detecting bugs and optimizing opportunities prior to implementation. The established Hoare logic offers a means to express assertions about program execution, albeit requiring manual specification which poses a considerable challenge. Conversely, programmatic definitions often diverge from conventional Hoare logic specifications due to their abstract nature, necessitating either domain-specific tool assistance or domain knowledge. Nevertheless, researchers have devised methods to streamline this process, including reverse static analysis, which extracts logic-based invariants from program definitions, thereby streamlining software verification aspects. This paper introduces an innovative technique to extract Hoare logic-based assertions from functional domain definitions via reverse static analysis, specifically targeting the Java functional programming subset of SeL4 Linux R4-2020, a widely used R4 version of the Linux runtime system that runs on over 60% of servers under the Cloud Init dashboard. The extracted logic specifications prove effective for facilitating discussions among software developers concerning program execution.

A critical challenge in achieving consensus among distributed systems is the consensus protocol, which underpins applications like distributed databases and distributed blockchains. The Canopus protocol, a cutting-edge solution, enables reaching consensus among innumerable nodes within a limited time frame, even with numerous failed attempts. However, the current implementation of Canopus has a limitation in its message handling capabilities due to its single-threaded, queue-based design. This paper proposes a high-performance, scalable message handling system for Canopus. Our solution, based on lock-free programming and the epoll mechanism, efficiently processes a vast number of messages. We achieved remarkable results with our system, scaling up to 100 million operations per second using just a single core, and demonstrated its scalability performance.

Recent studies have explored how the presence of cholesterol affects the elastic properties of lipid bilayers, particularly in relation to its role in membrane curvature. This work investigates the effect of cholesterol on the bending modulus by analyzing the thermal undulations of lipid bilayers with and without cholesterol, under free periodic boundary conditions. Cholesterol molecules were incorporated into simulations of pure DPPC lipid bilayers at three different concentrations to assess its impact on the bending modulus. This was done by comparing the simulation results with those of unstabilized DPPC bilayers, adjusted to similar areas per molecule. This comparison allowed for a more accurate analysis of how cholesterol affects the material properties and the structural organization of lipid bilayers. This work also examines how these changes relate to the overall stability and order of lipid bilayers.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model, specifically its ability to represent a universe with finite density, and compares its loop effects to those predicted by quantum gravity theory. Our analysis reveals that in a universe modeled by loop quantum cosmology, the point at which critical matter density occurs and the point at which quantum gravity effects become significant do not coincide. Unlike general relativity, this universe modeled by loop quantum cosmology does not undergo a gradual transition from classical to quantum behavior but instead experiences the onset of quantum effects at its critical density.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalogued 14 high-energy cosmic rays (> 10 EeV) not seen in the Northern hemisphere, focusing on two key events originating from the south-west. What appeared as showers had only three particles entering the detector's core region due to the extensive nature of the events. An analysis of data from multiple detectors revealed these events' key characteristics and confirmed they belonged to the highest-energy events ever recorded. ANA-2 and ANA-3, the events in question, were recorded during the Auger's spring observation in 2013. These high-energy events show a preference for the south-west, and were likely triggered by the X-3 event a few days prior. These newly recorded events will be incorporated into the analysis of anemalous events published earlier.

Deep neural networks have become a popular approach for complex robotic systems due to their robustness. Nevertheless, neural networks often produce excessive output noise, particularly when dealing with sensor data, which is highly sensitive to slight variations. This unpredictability in output is a major concern, which is being explored through the development of neural ensemble uncertainty quantification techniques. These innovative methods utilize multiple neural networks to generate point estimates and variance in their predictions, thereby offering valuable insights into the reliability of their predictions and the surrounding environment, as demonstrated in a robotic arm experiment involving vision-based gripper opening-angle estimation.

The integration of advanced traffic information systems has led to significant advancements in traffic monitoring and prediction. Modern deep learning-based prediction models have achieved notable success in predicting traffic speed, but their susceptibility to translation invariance issues poses a challenge when applied to real-world traffic data. This sensitivity can cause them to be easily misled by non-representative information within the data. To address this limitation, a novel approach called CV-GLP is proposed, which utilizes Glowing Pixel-Lattice Models to capture traffic speed patterns while maintaining translation invariance. This method also enables it to filter out misleading information by detecting non-informative crop patches, thereby enhancing predictions' robustness and interpretability. Experimental results demonstrate that CV-GLP surpasses state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy and robustness, while exhibiting superior performance in handling non-representative data and eliminating misleading information. Furthermore, CV-GLP outperforms existing models in speed prediction, time-series classification, and traffic speed anomaly detection tasks.

In recent years, rewriting systems for strict Gray categories have been developed and enhanced. However, creating equivalent rewriting systems for general tricategories has proven challenging due to difficulties in selecting suitable equational axioms for pentagon diagrams. We address this issue by creating a comprehensive set of weakening principles for tricategories, presented in a diagrammatic format. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these principles can be applied to simplify complex expressions in strict Gray categories and generalized examples, ultimately making it easier to verify equality between composites of tetrahedron diagrams.

Segmentation of the hippocampus using the manual method is a laborious task and cannot be performed on large populations. A computerized solution is required to diagnose neuropsychiatric disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, which is characterized by hippocampus atrophy. To address this issue, we present a fully automated, accurate, and robust pipeline for hippocampus segmentation, which relies on a deep fully convolutional neural network, as well as a novel loss function called 'DICE-IOU loss'. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, which include U-Net, Mask R-CNN, Res2Net, and Inception3-Res2Net. U-Net, specifically, serves as the comparison baseline, which we compared to in terms of efficiency and accuracy. Our evaluation, which utilized three public datasets, the Subjective Integrity of Memory and Spatial Cognition dataset, and toTAL Memory dataset, as well as OASIS open access dataset, highlights the superiority of our novel loss function, which led to improved accuracy and reduced training time compared to the cross-entropy loss function, which outperformed U-Net in terms of efficiency and accuracy.

We've developed an experiment to explore the quantum effect of single photons occupying two separate paths involving three parties. Our model illustrates that when no two of these parties share a path at a time, interference patterns emerge even without entanglement, and our data shows this quantum behavior follows logical rules for the rules governing our superposition states. Additionally, even classically generated light exhibits this behavior, confirming that it can be explained using non-qubit quantum theory.

Our research identifies the primary factor influencing the intensity of the inner proton radiation belt as the $C_{32}$ gravitational potential term from PAWL model data. This finding is based on the analysis of how this term affects the high-harmonic space proton trajectories using the Fokker-Planck equation, particularly in relation to adiabatic invariant $I_3$. By mapping high-harmonic space proton trajectories with and without the $C_{32}$ term, we observed that its inclusion expands the region of stable motion, aligning with recent inner belt observations from XPAC experiment results on board CHAMP satellite.

A network's ability to learn certain tasks is influenced by its expressiveness, which is tied to architectural limitations and has been a key factor in determining performance ceilings for deep neural networks. Recent studies have focused on various expressiveness definitions, which have been proposed by different researchers. This paper examines the connections between expressiveness definitions X.1 through X.5 in the context of multivariate functions. Although existing expressiveness definitions have primarily been applied to Euclidean space, this study extends one particular definition (X.5) to be valid across arbitrary metric spaces. As a result, this paper derives a hierarchy of expressiveness definitions, showing that if a deep neural network model satisfies definition X.5 in a given setting, it will also satisfy definitions X.1 through X.4 in the same setting.

This research focuses on developing a universally applicable strategy for low-rank matrix completion in an environment where external influences are uncertain and the data is compromised. A novel algorithm based on the Huber loss is introduced and shown to be both robust and achieving an optimal error rate, even when the dataset is intercepted. Furthermore, a differential privacy mechanism is designed to safeguard user data, with the study demonstrating that this algorithm remains efficient and stable when optimal settings for its parameters are chosen.

We propose a novel approach to modeling interstellar dust where larger grains are composed of a mixture of traditional silicate and carbon-based materials, along with large polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), which also contribute to the previously thought 'interstellar scission band'. This new model also explains observed asymmetries in dust composition through competition between PAH and acCRETION on larger grains, which also influences the production of PAH itself, potentially explaining fluctuations in its presence. Our comprehensive model accurately replicates observed silicate absorption, interstellar extinction patterns and production rates of dust components, indicating that present-day star formation rates are an inherent outcome of these interstellar processes, which also predicts specific features such as certain elemental ratios, time-dependent elemental variations, and distinct characteristics of produced PAHs. These features can be used to track dust production in the universe and help predict future production of heavy stars and elements in an evolving universe.

Consider the following light switch puzzle defined on a graph with $n$ vertices, where a subset of vertices has lights turned on initially. A unique property is that pressing the button on a lit vertex either always or never toggles the light status of its connected vertices - this characteristic defines the graph as a switching configuration graph. This paper establishes that a switching configuration graph is applicable to any initial configuration where it is possible to turn off all lights. Moreover, it addresses the computational complexity of finding a sequence of button presses to solve such a puzzle by exploring its linear programming duality and identifying when it can be efficiently resolved using linear programming. Additionally, this analysis enables solving the switching configuration puzzle in $O(n)$ time for graphs containing a cycle and is accompanied by a corresponding algorithm with an expected time complexity of $O(n)$. This paper also investigates the computational complexities of related problems including identifying all valid button presses and counting the total number of sequences that can turn off all lights.

This paper presents a novel, two-stage image segmentation model, OLISA, that incorporates image restoration capabilities to accurately delineate objects even when they are obscured. Initially, the model enhances image clarity through a specially designed image restoration module that utilizes semantic information to remove noise. Following this enhancement, the model transitions to segmenting the object of interest with its boundary detection module. Both components work synergistically to form a cohesive system that refines the segmentation outcomes through mutual iteration. As a result, the proposed OLISA model achieves superior boundary accuracy and segment coherence compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches on multiple challenging segmentation tasks where objects are heavily affected by noise.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the program's infinite semantic behavior using finite approximations. The computation of these approximations is typically split into two stages: an inner stage that improves an initial approximation by refining it based on the program's semantics, and an outer stage that ensures the refined approximations are sufficiently coarse to be computable. The accuracy of the analysis depends on when the inner stage is stopped. An iterative process that uses the program's syntax to analyze its structure and determine the likelihood of a fine-grained approximation being reached can help decide when to stop the inner stage.

In recent years, topological phonons have received significant attention due to their occurrence within specific phononic crystal and mechanical system arrays. Their presence has also been found within the more complex real-material structures such as Laves phases, hexagonal close-packed compounds, and perovskites, primarily consisting of heavier elements. Our study reveals that topological phonons are more widespread within their corresponding lighter element counterparts, namely hydrogen-filled Laves phases, hexagonal close-packed hydrides, and perhydros. Furthermore, we have also found that the presence of topological phonons can be induced in harmonic phononic systems without any structural modifications by incorporating electronic vertex corrections into them. These findings demonstrate that topological phonons can be prevalent within a wider variety of systems and can be generated through various mechanisms.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various real-world applications is increasingly critical. One established approach, using distance-based methods, stands out for not requiring specific data distribution assumptions and accommodating high-dimensional data. These techniques rely on the principle that as data points move away from a reference point, their local environment becomes more uniform randomly, making them effective in identifying anomalies. Despite the established theory, there has been a lack of comprehensive empirical analysis to support these ideas and make them more widely accepted in the practical data science community. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by evaluating the performance of different variants of distance-based outlier detection methods and related techniques, such as isolation forest, using a wide range of synthetic, real-world data sets and varying anomaly difficulty levels. The results, supported by both statistical analysis and human assessment, show that distance-based methods are competitive with other state-of-the-art methods, especially in certain scenarios. The study also reveals significant performance disparities among these algorithms. Ultimately, the research aims to provide a more in-depth understanding of the relative strengths and weaknesses of these methods, promoting transparency and making knowledge more accessible to the global data science community.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic quantum field containing a uniformly excited atomic source near a perfectly conducting plane using a Wick-rotated background free Bose field theory in canonical quantization. These findings replicate previously obtained rates for a more comprehensive model that accounts for the atom's motion and interaction in a rotated background. These models are based on a non-relativistic mass operator that describes a dipole-moment interaction between a spin-1/2 particle and a Bose field. The dipole-moment interaction mimics the effect of a quantum electric dipole, which emerges from a quantum electric dipole operator in a more rigorous quantum electrodynamics approach by Feynman and Hibbs.

As applications of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) grow, the focus on GNN's fairness has grown, despite the lack of a unified definition. Network fairness, which evaluates a predictor's fairness in relation to a graph's network structure, presents unique challenges. Prior research has primarily examined fairness with respect to individual attributes, neglecting the possibility of considering an aggregated attribute. In this work, we address this gap by exploring the fairness implications of combining multiple sensitive attributes to form a composite contextually relevant fair group. Moreover, we address the challenge of achieving fairness when nodes' labels are unreliable due to biases or errors, which is another concern overlooked by previous research. Our proposed framework, AdjGNN, addresses these concerns by incorporating a graph convolutional network to capture spatial context and introducing a novel fairness metric that balances accuracy and fairness. The optimized AdjGNN model, which leverages an adversarial autoencoder to ensure model robustness and resistance to bias-driven unfairness, significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art models in fairness-related metrics on synthetic and real-world datasets.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The resulting approximations demonstrate a high degree of accuracy when compared to exact numerical solutions to these models.

A newly proposed search method to detect gluinos is introduced, applicable when they decay into light particles through virtual intermediate squark states. By exploiting the characteristics of the end points in scalar particle mass distributions, this approach retains the standard gluino search's excellent signal to background performance. Simultaneously, it significantly expands the range of the supersymmetry mass spectrum that can be investigated. Specifically, the gluino mass that can be searched for is halved when the gluino mass itself is doubled, or when the squark mass that gluinos interact with is increased. As a result, the proposed method enables the investigation of a gluino mass nearly five times the mass of top and bottom quarks, assuming the mass difference between the two is at least ten times the top and bottom quark masses' sum. Likewise, the proposed method allows for the investigation of squark masses nearly forty times the mass of the gluino, under similar conditions. Furthermore, the proposed method relies on a nearly standard background rejection technique and maintains its performance even when scalar particle interactions are turned off through the so-called non-terminating spectrum. As such, the proposed method is a crucial addition to the existing search methods for supersymmetry. As a result, it serves as an essential tool for the ongoing search for supersymmetry at the Large Hadron Collider.

Our theory explains the formation and fluctuations of financial bubbles as a result of varying beliefs and strategies among market arbitrageurs. This divergence in trading behavior gives rise to new, shared beliefs that can contribute to the creation of bubbles. We've identified the necessary conditions for the appearance, coexistence, and disappearance of financial bubbles. Specifically, our model suggests that reduced risk tolerance, low risk-free interest rates, low expected market returns, and low risk among arbitrageurs can lead to bubble formation. However, it's also the reduced risk among arbitrageurs that ultimately contributes to their disappearance.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that change over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matching simulations using the variational quantum simulator. This included examining how the phase space evolves over time under different forces, with a particular emphasis on when oscillatory behavior occurs, either with or without complex phases. Furthermore, in the time-varying force simulation, we investigated phase space transformations and observed phenomena such as squeezing and the alteration of oscillation amplitude.

This study proposes a novel hybrid recommender system that integrates sentiment analysis to enhance the accuracy of product rating predictions. The traditional approach in recommender systems often relies on historical rating data, but can be hindered by noise from reviews unrelated to product quality. By contrast, leveraging the output of a BERT-based sentiment classifier enables the noise-filtered rating prediction model to deliver more precise quality-based recommendations. Furthermore, our framework optimizes its underlying neural networks through a semi-supervised learning method, combining unsupervised sentiment classification and supervised rating prediction to improve overall performance. The effectiveness of our approach is substantiated through extensive experimentation on multiple well-known public datasets.

This paper presents a novel model to address the code-switching challenge within NLP by utilizing Neural Machine Translation. One significant obstacle to overcoming code-switching is the scarcity of annotated data, particularly bilingual or multilingual texts. To overcome this limitation, we propose using Neural Machine Translation as a means of expanding and annotating texts across languages. Our approach involves developing a novel model called ENM-T, which performs a novel machine translation task of switching between annotation languages. To further improve the effectiveness of code-switching tasks, we introduce a new loss function based on the switch sensitivity of the switch tag and a corresponding attention mechanism. Our results indicate that trained ENM-T models can serve as a pre-processing step to enhance the performance of downstream NLP tasks involving code-switching, and that our proposed model and techniques yield substantial improvements over existing approaches.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on products of group- and coset-spaces, which are generalized versions of lambda deformations. Utilizing a sigma-model approach, first, we identify the constraints needed to ensure the model's integrability after applying a D-brane's influence, which are represented by a specific type of matrix at the boundary. Next, we identify solutions to these constraints that yield conformally invariant branes in the models' product structures. Our analysis covers both product expansions of currents and products of currents with their Hermitian conjugates, encompassing various brane types found in the literature, which include conformal brane solutions related to D3-branes in certain deformations of $AdS_5 \times S^5$. Furthermore, we confirm previous findings of integrable conformal brane solutions in the product of two circles model and our research broadens to include similar solutions in the higher-dimensional version of the same theory. Our findings suggest a more extensive set of D-brane solutions to be found within this class of theories that maintain integrability.
