The CDF II collaboration has recently found a significant discrepancy between the measured mass of the W boson and the predicted mass based on the Standard Model. Specifically, the measured mass is 0.00306 times the square of the Z boson's mass plus or minus 0.00038 and has a 7.1 sigma deviation from the predicted mass. The measured mass is 0.00786 times the square of the Z boson's mass plus or minus 0.00038 and has a 7.1 sigma deviation from the predicted mass. In response, the ATLAS collaboration has proposed a new W' model that can potentially resolve this issue. The proposed model predicts that the W' can be detected when the transverse momentum of the W' is around 1 TeV. A proposed International Linear Collider (ILC) has the potential to detect such a W' particle by measuring its production cross-section or by directly probing its mass. Specifically, the ILC can detect a W' with a mass up to 2.5 TeV by measuring its production cross-section or by directly probing its mass. Such a detection is feasible within a reasonable amount of luminosity, specifically, 1 ab^-1 per year over a period of five years.

Software developers face difficulties in choosing relevant search terms for identifying similar projects when selecting appropriate information from change requests can be challenging and time-consuming. In software development, software scientists also struggle to find applicable search terms for their research on the identification of analogous search targets, where researchers often have to select applicable search terms manually, which can be a tedious task. In this context, our objective is to automate search term suggestion for researchers by leveraging the principles of information retrieval and collective intelligence to suggest relevant terms based on their field of study and related keywords.

In human interaction, individuals' emotional states and vocal tones naturally converge. This study explores whether artificial intelligence models can also establish a similar convergence. We've created a new model that can learn this convergence through a unique training method that forces two artificial intelligence components to work together. This method has yielded positive outcomes by demonstrating significant improvements in conversation realness when one component generates text and both components are used for analysis. Furthermore, our results show that this model can also learn to match a speaker's emotional state and vocal tone through metrics measuring these factors.

We've developed an open-source suite of Seagle simulations, widely utilized in the study of galaxy spectra, stellar populations, and photometry. The code performs detailed spectral energy distribution modeling, enabling researchers to determine properties of galaxies, star clusters, and galaxies in the early universe, as well as to plan JWST observations by predicting optimal configurations for detecting specific emission lines or maximizing transmission efficiency in photometric mode. The project's primary goal is to make efficient use of data reduction techniques by utilizing various filtering techniques, including continuum, photometric, and line-based filters tailored to the James Webb Space Telescope's instruments. Our approach also includes the option to compare simulated observations against actual observations, thereby facilitating the differentiation of Seagle's output from genuine data and enabling the optimization of observation strategies. This paper will outline our methodology and demonstrate how to generate Seagle simulations and create filtering techniques for these simulations.

Classifying every video frame can be extremely difficult, particularly when classes are predefined. This challenge is often addressed by using class-defined or class-less definitions, also known as functional segmentation, where the goal is to identify specific video events without predefining all possible classes. This research presents Segmentation by Spatial and Temporal Consistency among Parts, an unsupervised approach designed to identify distinct video regions across multiple frames without relying on class definitions. This technique outperforms current state-of-the-art definitions in both class-defined and functional segmentation, demonstrating its adaptability across a range of applications.

We explore the existence of seven hadronic molecular states consisting of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, create their mass spectra, investigate their production through J/ψ p collision, and examine their decays into the $J/\psi N$ final state. The investigation leverages theoretical frameworks, incorporating the one-gluon exchange one-gluon exchange model and S-wave projection, to determine the production cross-sections. By identifying $\bar D \Sigma_c$ as a benchmark, we determine key parameters for production rates. Our analysis reveals $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$ production cross-sections comparable to those of $\bar D \Sigma_c$, with the $\bar D \Sigma_c$ being a possible $I = 1$ or $I = 0$ hadronic molecular state. The production cross-section ratios of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$ to $\bar D \Sigma_c$ can serve as crucial evidence for these exotic hadronic molecular states, making them viable targets for experimental research at the D0SP P experiment.

The widespread adoption of information technology has made software testing concepts essential knowledge for students, yet current education methods often rely on traditional lecturing, which has been found less effective compared to alternative learning approaches. A novel approach has been developed to teach testing concepts through interactive, inquiry-based learning, combining theoretical knowledge with practical applications in an engaging environment. This method has been implemented in university courses and its effectiveness compared to traditional teaching methods. Evaluation results indicate that students using this new approach had a deeper understanding of testing concepts, enjoyed the learning experience more, and felt they acquired valuable life skills, while also demonstrating improved test design capabilities.

Domain adaptation, a key area of machine learning, aims to enhance model performance by utilizing large amounts of unlabeled data from diverse domains. This research explores making cross-domain adaptation more accessible to researchers without machine learning expertise by developing a user-friendly, Python-based interface called Value-DomADP. Based on the COMADR domain decomposition method, the proposed inter-domain regularization technique, Value-FDA, achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple 3D datasets. Furthermore, the method's effectiveness is extended to a semi-supervised mutual enhancement approach, yielding stronger performance in cross-domain adaptation tasks. Additionally, the domain adaptation tool is applied to 3D shape recovery and multi-label 3D segmentation, yielding impressive quantitative outcomes. Ultimately, the technique and its accompanying software enable non-experts to easily apply it in their work.

A compact and efficient core is proposed for a gas core reactor that could achieve high power density, by incorporating a gas-driven Brayton cycle. To enhance power output and thermal efficiency, a two-stage Brayton cycle is implemented. An numerical simulation model is developed for conducting parametric studies. The results show the power density can be optimized through adjustments of the flow area, pressure ratio, and intercooling temperature in the proposed reactor.

This paper introduces a new deep learning approach for particle physics experiments by leveraging knowledge from the Standard Model to enhance Domain Adversarial Neural Networks. The proposed method, DiNN, utilizes a domain knowledge layer containing 1200 particle interaction interactions that are integrated into the domain adversarial multilayer perceptron framework. The result is a model with higher localization accuracy while requiring fewer parameters compared to a standard multilayer perceptron.

The accuracy of spectral models for substellar objects depends on a variety of factors, including their atmospheric properties, bond albedos, and molecular cross-sections. Specifically, small variations in the absorption cross-section of water vapor, which is the dominant absorber, can lead to significant discrepancies in the predicted spectral features. To address this, we used the BOLO code to model the spectra of T dwarfs, incorporating different self-consistent bond albedo calculations and varying cross-sections from multiple sources for water vapor, as well as variations in other atmospheric parameters. Our simulations revealed that the interplay between the cross-section of water and temperature-pressure profiles and cloud pressure greatly affects the interdependence of spectral features. Furthermore, we found that the choice of bond albedo calculation method significantly impacts the sensitivity of the spectral features to cross-section variations. To address these uncertainties, we developed a pressure-cloud model and applied it to the analysis of the L9.5 Dornadotti-Bernal system, which has been characterized by varying cross-sections and pressure configurations.

This text offers an in-depth explanation of the theoretical underpinnings of variable instantiation in Answer Set Programming. We build upon ASP's modeling language semantics to define a formal description of grounding algorithms using well-established operators. Our formal framework is validated by providing constructive proofs of several key properties and by developing a range of grounding operators across established grounding methods. This unified perspective enables us to identify novel operators in XSD2ASP, an innovative incremental grounding algorithm. We demonstrate that these newly introduced operators contribute to the efficiency of XSD2ASP in specific modeling scenarios.

We have extended quantum resource theories to encompass complex scenarios with multiple intertwined resources by establishing a generalized framework for them. In multi-resource scenarios, we found that relative entropy measures both the distance of any theory's invariant sets from the complementary space and serve as a lower bound on the cost of freely converting complex states back to their resource-intensive precursors. Furthermore, for theories with sets of polytope, we found for the first time the exact cost of free conversion for any situation with multiple constraints. We've applied our findings to the theory of thermodynamics, deriving a new expression for the cost of free conversion based on multi-dimensional energy limitations. We've also explored the relationship between our findings and the reverse triangle inequality of relative entropy, generating new inequalities along the way. We'll discuss our results in the context of existing literature on resource theories, with a focus on multi-dimensional applications, and we'll consider the broader implications of our research for the theoretical understanding of resources, with a particular emphasis on the thermodynamic theory. We'll wrap up the article by discussing the further generalizations of resource theories that we believe to be promising areas of further study.

This work investigates a relationship between two types of estimation error bounds.
While many information theories prioritize information measures over estimation tasks,
recent studies have successfully applied information theoretic tools to tight estimation error limits.
We establish that in certain channels, specifically those with symmetry,
a particular bound, the Positivity Minimum Mean-Square Error (PMMSE), equals the standard MSE when
odd moments are considered, due to the influence of symmetric channel properties.
We demonstrate a connection to time-reversal symmetry in physical systems.
We then relate the PMMSE to the concept of detailed balance.
We show that for channels following normal and compound normal distributions,
the PMMSE offers a tighter limit than the standard MSE, deriving an explicit formula for it.
We discuss how this bound influences estimators developed under information theoretic constraints.

We analyze how to identify unit root directions and covariance matrices for a specific matrix time series that exhibits first-order Markov behavior with a specific structure. These directions and the eigenvalues indicate the number of stochastic trends within the data and their respective long-term patterns. Given only access to the time series data $Y_t$, we propose estimation methods for key matrices based on empirical evidence. Our estimators demonstrate consistency with M-estimator theory, and the limiting distributions of our estimators are derived for various matrix functions. Additionally, a test is developed to assess whether a specific matrix function is positive definite. Our methods extend beyond previous approaches, allowing for the analysis of higher-order Markov processes.

A novel family of quantum low-density parity-check code families is introduced, characterized by a flexible trade-off between rate, distance, and distance-to-correct-threshold ratio. This is achieved through a novel construction using classical LDPC codes and a matrix product code approach, yielding rates of at least $1/d$ and ratios as high as $\tilde O(d)/n$ for large $n$. This outcome surpasses previously established bounds, namely the quantum LDPC threshold theorem and dual polar codes. The related code families include finite distance LDPC quantum codes with constant ratio, rates, and linear growth; those meeting the quantum LDPC threshold theorem; rate and ratio both equal to $1/d$; and nearly optimal ratio of $d/\tilde n$ within the constraints of the quantum LDPC threshold theorem.

The distance-$r$ dominating set problem, abbreviated as DrDS, seeks the smallest subset of vertices in a graph, $D$, such that every other vertex in the graph is at a distance of at most $r$ from a vertex in $D$. DrDS generalizes the $k$-center problem, a well-known NP-hard problem, making many DrDS problems NP-hard as well. When the parameter $r$ is fixed, several specific problems, like DrDS on interval graphs, semi-circle graphs, and strongly chordal graphs, have been solved efficiently. Conversely, DrDS on $k$-tree graphs remains an open question despite being solvable in a linear time complexity for each $r$. In this research, we provide an algorithmic solution, achieving a linear time complexity of $O_r(n)$, for DrDS on $r$-VSP graphs, where previous work demonstrated a quadratic time complexity of $O_r(n^2)$ for the related VCSP problem.

This research examines the impact of disorder on two-dimensional topological insulators of higher-order topology, focusing on how it influences their topological characteristics in a real-world context. Our findings reveal that disorder does not undermine the topological properties being studied, as indicated by a complete separation of states in the system's effective Hamiltonian. We also identify a metric correlation length that indicates the typical size of the system's internal states in various levels of disorder. Notably, we discover that disorder modifies the intensity of systems' internal states by reducing the global topological parameter's value in direct proportion to the amount of disorder present. Ultimately, our research confirms the existence of unique states in the system that are shielded by the correlation length's influence and remain pinball-localized even when surrounded by a sea of states.

Recent searches for supersymmetry at the electroweak scale have been reported by the CMS experiment in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, analyzed through three distinct studies based on the data collected in 2016. These searches specifically looked for signs of heavy gluinos that decay into lighter top quarks and photons/neutrinos, leaving signatures of objects such as jets, photons, and missing transverse energy. No significant deviation from expected background levels was detected in the data. No supersymmetry models were excluded at 95% confidence level. The results of the search led to the exclusion of gluino-superpartner pairs, with masses up to 1.11 TeV and 660 GeV for the gluino and gluino-superpartner pairs, respectively. These pairs surpass the previous results from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations in the same supersymmetry scenario.

Novel view synthesis from unoccupied viewpoints remains an open challenge in computer graphics due to the inherent ill-posed nature of the problem. This challenge becomes even more pronounced when dealing with real-world images captured by consumer cameras that lack intrinsic geometric information. This paper presents a data-driven approach leveraging a neural radiance field model trained on real-world single-perspective images with unknown camera intrinsics. This model both determines camera properties and produces novel views any number of rotations away from the original viewpoint. By representing the light field in four-dimensional space, the approach enables efficient synthesis of novel views through simple linear operations, thus requiring fewer training shots and further allowing for faster evaluation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets, surpassing previous techniques in both quality and latency, ultimately enabling real-time evaluation.

Our close-by observation of the binary system V470 Tau reveals the orbital movement of both stars. Based on astrometric data from 2018 to 2020, we've established V470 Tau's orbital parameters, including the time of periastron passage and the magnitude of the second star, approximately 0.46 solar radii. Furthermore, we've analyzed the system's orbital eccentricity and the influence of the stars' spin axes on the orbit, as well as the possibility of a third, unseen body within the system.

In the context of the colour-kinematics duality in self-dual gravity, we identify an area-preserving diffeomorphism algebra within the SDW formalism. This is analogous to the Lie algebra found in the Fock representation. Utilizing the universal central extension, we establish the corresponding Lie algebraic structure. This is then applied to the Weyl tensor to define the gravitational field strength in the self-dual sector, resulting in the identification of the Witten equation as the zero-mode condition of the Jacobi identity. Utilizing Green's function methods, we determine the solution to the Witten equation, which enables the construction of the classical action using the method of the double copy. Ultimately, we obtain the solution, which is a key component in the self-dual Chern-Simons type action for the self-dual graviton. This derivation holds the potential for the extension of the duality in the full theory of gravity to be explored.

A powerful and sudden increase in radio signals known as a "burst" can occur on the Sun, typically triggered by shock waves generated during solar eruptions called flares. These radio bursts, specifically type II bursts, are often associated with the coronal mass ejections (CMEs) that are launched from the Sun. To study the Sun's impact on Earth, scientists have been using the Kodaikanal Solar Radio Spectrometer (KSRS) to study type II bursts. In this research, the KRSRS was able to detect two distinct radio bursts on the Sun on January 17, 2022, that originated from shock waves produced by CMEs. These radio signals were characterized by specific features such as steep type II bursts with short durations and strong signals. To study the characteristics of the radio signals, the KRSRS data was analyzed and combined with other observational data, such as solar observations from space-based missions. To study the characteristics of the radio signals, the KRSRS data was analyzed using specific techniques for studying the characteristics of the signals. A comprehensive analysis in the general two Higgs doublet model has been conducted, where the model's parameters are adjusted to match observed anomalies in unusual B meson decays. This has led to a single point in the model's parameter space where the decays of B mesons fit the data, but does not include radiative corrections. The model's predictions for rare B meson processes are then examined and found to be inconsistent with a 2σ confidence level. Further examining real world data, particularly from L3 and BaBar, shows the anomalies in certain B meson decay ratios conflict. However, when only combining data from L3 and BaBar's radiative decay observations, the model helps to explain the anomalies.

This study introduces a unique, self-contained three-dimensional random vortex system that mirrors the behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations for non-viscous incompressible fluid flows. The newly developed random vortex system incorporates a stochastic differential equation that interacts with a pair of non-linear coupled deterministic differential equations through duality in their conditional distributions. The creation of this random vortex system relies on the technique of Donsker-Revuz representation, applied to space-time vortex equations as a new type of non-local non-linear partial differential equation. The approach involves solving time-dependent vortex equations and utilizing their non-local Poisson equation form, enabling the establishment of the random vortex system with a key duality property in its conditional distributions. The method also establishes a connection between the random vortex system and non-linear vortex equations as a non-local non-linear partial differential equation as well as a weak solution to the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations. The random vortex system may offer valuable insights into random modeling of partial differential equations, particularly in fluid dynamics, and contributes to a novel weak solution method for three-dimensional non-linear partial differential equations through the application of stochastic techniques.

The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely generated using S single photons passed through beam splitters with N modes, yielding an almost uniform distribution of output patterns. Our work aims to measure the maximum entropy of boson sampling process by analyzing the information gained after observing a few measurement outcomes. We find that observing just L patterns, where L << N, results in a maximum entropy of around ln[(N - D)/L + 1], confirming that boson sampling efficiently encodes mode information. Our findings demonstrate that boson sampling can serve as a random number generator requiring minimal measurements, and the acquired information can be leveraged to verify boson sampling with a relatively small number of acquired patterns, thus reducing the necessity for a large number of sampling runs.

Temporal sequence analysis is a crucial aspect of many real-world applications.
While temporal sequence data often exhibits low-dimensional structures,
existing dimension reduction techniques like SGTM-TT, though effective,
frequently require substantial computational resources to achieve optimal results.
In this study, we propose accelerating sgtm-tt with Nesterov momentum (a gradient
descent variant) to enhance its efficiency without compromising accuracy.
SGTM-TT, distinct from classical unsupervised Topographic Mapping, offers an alternative
for temporally ordered data with low-dimensional structure and labeled outcomes.
SGTM-TT excels in capturing temporal dependencies between input variables and output predictions,
maintaining relative ordering relationships within the embedded data.
We validate the proposed method's efficacy on temporal sequence datasets from
temporal clinical data and time series classification tasks.

Reinforcement learning seeks to develop agents that can maximize their long-term rewards through interactions with complex environments. The key challenge is efficiently navigating the vast action space to find optimal policies. Deep Reinforcement Learning methods have made significant progress by combining function approximation techniques, like Deep Q-Network, with reinforcement learning algorithms such as Monte-Carlo. Newer approaches, like GRU-DRL, leverage the GRU network architecture in reinforcement learning algorithms. We explore the potential of GRU-dRL in solving OpenAI Gym environments. To further enhance performance, we introduce a novel algorithm called Consensus-Homing, an asynchronous consensus-based method for solving consensus problems. Consensus-Homing allows a network of agents to reach a consensus on specific states by applying learned policies, without the need for extensive agent-agent communication. The proposed Consensus-Homing approach demonstrates improved return rates on OpenAI Gym environments, outperforming existing deep reinforcement learning algorithms, including those from the DRL-Baselines library, in our experiments.

In video action detection, current approaches primarily rely on temporal context extraction from visual features and spatial action context from scene relationships, whereas our novel approach combines these two types of context to improve action detection accuracy. We introduce a novel temporal-spatial action context that emphasizes spatiotemporal focus on action regions and their movements, thus highlighting key space-time action characteristics. Our approach employs a novel three-network network that learns visual features, spatial action context, and temporal focus on action movement, thus improving action detection accuracy. Our approach successfully integrates all context features to extract space-time action regions and focus on action movement, thus highlighting the importance of actions. Our novel approach successfully achieves first-ever action detection accuracy on UCF101 dataset with MAP@10 and UCF101+dataset with MAP@10 and UCF101+dataset with MAP@10 scores of 49.2% and 59.2% respectively, outperforming current state-of-the-art approaches by 3.2% and 4.3% respectively. Our approach successfully highlights actions and their movements, thus highlighting the importance of actions.

A recent study introduced a comprehensive dataset, specifically designed to evaluate and train copy detection algorithms. The dataset, labeled Copy-Dataset, is dynamically growing and includes images with deliberate copy-paste transformations. By analyzing the characteristics of the Copy-Dataset, we have identified the primary factors contributing to image transformations and their difficulties. Our analysis also highlights the effects of common image modifications on these transformations, and we propose an alternative, multi-step process to create more realistic and diverse training images.

Our research investigates the probabilistic behavior of stochastic processes in response to small-scale external influences in the vicinity of stable states. We have developed an approximate description of the process's trajectory over extended periods, in the limit of vanishingly small perturbations. Our analysis revealed that the dynamics of this trajectory depend on the specific size of the perturbation, with the process exhibiting metastability when the perturbation's size becomes sufficiently small. Moreover, this trajectory approximation enables a precise estimation of the perturbed process's rate of transition between stable states and a quantifiable asymptotic discrepancy from its actual behavior. We further applied our findings to a concrete scenario: the Brownian motion within a periodically structured environment with a gradually decreasing amplitude.

This study explores the influence of strong magnetic fields on the nucleon chemical potential within nuclear matter, focusing on its impact on the nucleon chemical potential's dependence on the quark chemical potential. Through calculations using the color-flavor-antisymmetry (CFA) model, we analyzed the spin polarization of nucleons and the behavior of the nucleon chemical potential under varying magnetic fields and quark chemical potentials. Our results indicate that strong magnetic fields significantly polarize nucleons and increase the nucleon chemical potential, thereby affecting its sensitivity to quark chemical potential.

Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have successfully integrated two key strategies: selective training and encrypted communication. Building on this foundation, we have developed a novel approach, called Selective Private Federated Learning (SPFEL), which enables the efficient training and accurate recovery of neural networks in decentralized environments, where data is scarce and sensitive. Our contributions encompass theoretical guarantees, a protocol specification, and practical implementations using a PyTorch framework. Our empirical results, based on experiments with artificial and real-world datasets (MNIST and CIFAR-10), demonstrate that SPFEL achieves exceptional model accuracy even with limited client data, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashish-krk/SPFEL-pytorch.

A comprehensive study of dark clouds, including their physical and chemical properties, can be significantly enhanced by the use of far-ultraviolet (FUV) spectroscopy. To observe dark clouds, the \textit{HST} FUV spectrograph was utilized, which was able to study four dark clouds, specifically Taurus, Serpens South, Ophiuchus, and Boogwa, at wavelengths of 115-160 nm. By utilizing \textit{IRIS} space-borne FUV images, it was determined that the \textit{HST} FUV spectrum in the far UV is not contaminated by scattered light from the \textit{IRIS} satellite. Furthermore, it was discovered that the \textit{HST} FUV spectrum in the far UV is composed of an underlying continuum and a series of emission lines. To separate the underlying continuum and emission lines, it was hypothesized that the underlying continuum is the result of \textit{H2} fluorescence and the emission line spectrum is the result of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. By \textit{HST} FUV spectrum analysis, it was observed that the \textit{H2} fluorescence is the main source of the \textit{H2} emission lines, which indicates that the \textit{H2} fluorescence is the main source of the \textit{H2} emission lines. Structured tables in various fields, particularly in science, efficiently present complex information in a compact format. However, the standard table extraction methods fall short, often requiring extensive manual review and editing to retain crucial content in the desired output. This paper presents ALaRIA, an advanced zero-shot algorithm for extracting table structures, leveraging structural and linguistic cues from BERT and spaCy parsers to achieve accurate results. By presenting enhanced parse trees and employing a compact set of specialized labels, ALaRIA achieves a 76% structured F1 score, surpassing prior methods in the field by 16%. Additionally, the paper introduces TaBLEx, an improved dataset for benchmarking table-to-XML structure extraction, featuring diverse syntactic and semantic contexts for more accurate evaluation.

This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Lukacova-Frydman, Mallick, and Penta (2021), and explores its capacity to produce an equilibrium in multi-stage games of incomplete information. By examining the dynamic theory's underlying assumptions, the equilibrium concepts it implies, and these in relation to standard rationalizability and equilibrium models of incomplete information, we gain insight into its properties and limitations. Ultimately, we demonstrate that under mild conditions, the dynamic theory gives rise to a unique perfect equilibrium, even in complex settings such as three-player games with continuous type spaces.

Precise and up-to-date estimates of a country's population are vital for implementing vaccination strategies and designing social security policies, as well as for predicting infrastructure requirements. As part of our research, we've developed an innovative estimator for the population, rooted in two widely used methods and incorporating unique features that give it distinct advantages. This innovative estimator excels at handling small sample sizes while effectively mitigating issues of undercounting. In contrast to traditional approaches, it relies solely on publicly available data, making it easily replicable and applicable to various contexts. In a simulated environment, our proposed estimator demonstrated considerable improvements over conventional approaches in providing more accurate estimates. Additionally, we've successfully applied our estimator to six scenarios, yielding substantial enhancements in estimation accuracy.

Over the past ten years, researchers have developed novel methods to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data verification systems. These innovative structures go beyond traditional systems and recent proposals, enabling a significant reduction in such errors. Historically, researchers have focused on creating standalone systems with the ability to correct errors, separate from flow cytometry analysis in biology. Our contributions in this paper span three areas: (1) we test the performance of the new structures within storage protocols and the HyperCube framework to assess their applicability in real-time data analysis within flow cytometry; (2) by leveraging a flow cytometry dataset as a benchmark, we demonstrate how these new structures can efficiently and accurately replicate their functionality; (3) we showcase the potential applications of these new structures in a range of scenarios beyond biology, including cloud computing and internet search.

We study a model that combines a weakly interacting Bose-Einstein condensate, excitation by a strong laser and spin-exchange collisions, and focus on the process where photon association transforms pairs of spin-zero atoms into spin-full molecules. We find that this photon association remains relatively constant in magnitude and is minimally affected by spin-exchange collisions. Photon association collisions and collisions mediated by virtual energy levels can both play a significant role in determining the steady-state yield of atom-molecule composites formed from spin-zero atoms upon illumination by photons. Our research indicates that it may be possible to manage the relative contributions of these two types of collisions in determining the molecule-atom rate ratio. Ultimately, we aim to utilize the capabilities of BEC management and management of photon association parameters to achieve a desired rate of collision between atoms and molecules.

A multi-resolution SPH method for fluid-structure interactions has been developed, combining various techniques such as the multi-grid approach, different fluid and solid solvers, a novel contact algorithm, and a numerical framework for FSI problems. Its effectiveness and efficiency have been tested with several benchmark cases including a single solid block dropping into water, water wave simulations, and a solid block FSI case. Results from the simulation of a solid block dropping into water show a multi-grid acceleration effect, whereas SPH fluid-structure interactions resulted in no such benefit. However, the multi-grid approach's numerical stability was compromised when applying it to a single solid block's fluid-structure interaction. Additionally, the multi-grid approach was found to introduce inaccuracies caused by coupling errors between grids.

Within certain bounds, quantum computing provides substantial speed improvements for machine learning by employing quantum data structures that enable more efficient handling of data in exponential dimensions. Unfortunately, a crucial limitation prevents the extraction of stored data as classical information, hindering algorithms from exploiting their full potential. This paper resolves this challenge by introducing an alternative "kernel method" that leverages quantum data while in memory and allows for the approximation of inner products between arbitrary data vectors. This breakthrough facilitates the adaptation of conventional machine learning algorithms, such as gradient descent, to operate with quantum data without necessitating data unloading. As an example, this approach is used to develop a new learning algorithm with applications in quantum chemistry.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch was found to have limited text variability due to its fixed vocal tone and pitch range. This variation can be enhanced by replacing the fixed pitch with dynamically generated pitches from the FastPitch model's analysis-synthesis system. However, the standard pitch-shifting technique affects the speech timbre, which in turn degrades the quality when the pitch is shifted lower to make room for higher pitches. This issue arises because the algorithm increases spectral energy and alters its distribution. This article proposes a novel approach, combining FastPitch with H. Ince's pitch-shifting technique, to preserve the pitch and timbre. The technique involves shifting spectral energy without altering its distribution and maintains overall energy by adjusting the spectral centroid. Experimental outcomes on the VOCOD dataset reveal that the new algorithm yields better quality than the old one across various evaluation metrics.

This paper proposes a novel framework for evaluating video-based object tracking reasoning. It opline integrates an off-the-shelf person tracker to monitor objects throughout videos. Furthermore, the framework enables comprehensive evaluation of fundamental tracking capabilities such as object continuity, proximity monitoring, interline tracking, and identification of hidden objects. It extends object tracking reasoning into a 2D spatial-temporal framework, thus enabling a deeper understanding of observer engagement. The proposed framework assesses a range of challenging scenarios, including split-and-merge, occlusion, long-distance tracking, and multi-object following.

Our study investigates including effects of the light top partner and the top quark in Drell-Yan production on various TeV-scale observables. Specifically, we focus on how these effects influence low-energy measurements in proton-proton collisions and the cumulative impact on precision theory predictions. Our analysis shows that these impacts can be constrained by existing data and may help distinguish between the light top partner's Standard Model-like and non-Symmetric E6 characteristics. Additionally, our work demonstrates that these impacts on low-energy measurements can be accurately simulated using effective field theory methods and can potentially be tested through future high-energy proton-proton collisions at a prospective 100 TeV collider.

Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence Robots have gained popularity in various environments such as research facilities, libraries, and hospitals due to their ability to navigate through these spaces and interact with users regardless of distance. A crucial aspect of these robots' effectiveness is ensuring seamless and secure communication between the controller and the robot. This study focuses on assessing the Quality of Experience (QoE) for remote Telepresence Robot control and navigation. To this end, the research involves a series of experiments to determine the factors affecting QoE, including video streaming quality, control loop latency, and bandwidth. Furthermore, the investigation aims to identify the threshold of acceptable interruption times without significantly impacting QoE. Utilizing the Mean Opinion Score (MOS) and Quick Rate (QR) metrics, the study evaluates video streaming quality, while gathering both user-generated data and objective measurements. Ultimately, the results produced a comprehensive model correlating QoE to bandwidth, latency, and interrruption time variables.

In this study, we revisit the core features of the Bayesian adaptive Lasso method initially developed by Fan, Huang, Liu, and Zhou in 2011. This method was created for hierarchical models and linear regression models with hierarchical structures, where we focus on sparse coefficients and sparse precision structures. By employing Bayesian techniques, we establish that the Bayesian adaptive Lasso produces the same results as a frequentist large-sample approach for both hierarchical and non-hierarchical models with various regression coefficients. Furthermore, we examine a specific case with the most precise matrix as a parameter in hierarchical structures, finding the Bayesian adaptive Lasso effective in inducing sparse structures. Our study builds on prior research, incorporating Bayesian non-asymptotic results from Liu, Barber, and Yu in 2012. Our work demonstrates that the Bayesian large-sample properties observed enable a direct extension of these results to non-hierarchical models with missing data issues. Our research also shows that the Bayesian self-consistency results obtained enable a further extension of these findings to non-asymptotic settings.

The game Mafia, a popular social deduction game, relies heavily on the player's analytical and logical reasoning abilities to identify which faction they are aligned with - either Mafia or civilian, sometimes with the added complexity of the Vigilante's presence. Our Mafia variant incorporates specific rules that determine how game outcomes change in relation to the number of Mafia members present, which ranges up to the total game population. We found that as the game's rule-sets become more extensive, optimal Mafia members count to maximize the chances of victory for both Mafia and civilians, varies depending on the game's size and number of rounds, revealing considerable disparity in victory probabilities among different Mafia counts.

Several planetary systems contain multiple giant planets positioned relatively close together, often aligned in the same plane and rotating in the same direction as the inner planets. Our study examines how gas accretion by planets in a gas-rich protoplanetary disk, particularly planets located relatively close to each other and to their star, impacts their mass distribution. Through a series of simulations conducted using a model that tracks planetary migration, mass growth, and atmospheric composition, we examined various factors, including planet spacing, star distance, and the timing of gas accretion. Results from our simulations reveal that gas accretion durations of around 1-2 million years align with our current understanding of planetary formation. Furthermore, we observed that late-stage gas accretion tends to produce planets with larger masses relative to one another than early-stage accretion, suggesting that gas dynamics and planetary interactions may play significant roles in the formation of planetary mass ratios and final positions.

Understanding electrical conductivity in materials at a microscopic level is a significant challenge in the field of nanoelectronics, particularly when it comes to novel materials. Interactions between phonons and charge carriers play a significant role in both determining a material's electrical properties and limiting the effectiveness of electronic devices. By leveraging high-quality graphene nanoribbons in our experiments, we were able to precisely measure the effects of long-range interactions between acoustic phonons on electrical conductivity. Our findings align with a theoretical model based on the diagrams of self-energy and the vertex correction, thereby providing a reliable foundation for the accurate design of future nanoelectronic components.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in quality and relevance. It involves two key stages: (i) identifying feature weights to capture the importance of individual features, and (ii) identifying cluster centers. The k-means objective function is maximized in the first phase, and the Laplacian eigenmaps objective function is minimized in the second phase. Two critical challenges in the proposed approach are resolved using advanced optimization techniques: (i) identifying feature weights and (ii) dealing with missing data. Two validation datasets are used to test and validate the performance of the proposed method, with experimental findings demonstrating its superiority in handling complex, high-dimensional data.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become a key component in various advanced neural network designs, including those by DeepMind. Designing algorithms to learn MoE models' parameters poses a challenge, however. Established algorithms like EM1D and its derivatives are limited to near-optimal convergence under certain conditions, like low dimensionality and strong concentration properties, which often aren't met in practical settings. In this paper, we present new stochastic algorithms based on the EM method for learning MoE models. These algorithms can handle high-dimensional inputs and work well under weaker concentration properties. Theoretically, these algorithms converge to near-optimal solutions in nonconvex optimization and are robust to outliers in data, even with unbounded input distribution. The methods demonstrate superior performance in real-world settings across multiple nonconvex tasks, like learning MoE regression classes and multi-label classification, while also being efficient in terms of time complexity and suitable for large-scale applications.

This set of notes provides a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on Combinatorial Methods in Algebraic Geometry.

While global symmetries hold significant importance in Particle Physics and Cosmology, they cannot be realized in the Standard Model due to a fundamental flaw. We identify the source of this flaw and provide solutions, which could have significant implications for our understanding of dark matter.

Our research presents the first comprehensive study of the four Magellanic Globular Clusters, located in LMC and LMC2, uncovering a multitude of blue horizontal branch stars, including around 50 blue straggler candidates in each cluster. We analyze in detail the characteristics of stars that fall into three categories: blue horizontal branch, blue straggler, and blue giant branch. Our data collection process involved extracting a large amount of information from 292,892 cluster members, which we then categorized. We made a deliberate effort to avoid any initial categorization of these stars based on their properties. Our findings provide a more accurate and nuanced understanding of the star populations in these four Magellanic Globular Clusters. We analyze their properties, which aligns with the expectations for blue horizontal branch, blue straggler, and blue giant branch populations. Our research reveals a wealth of new insights into the properties of these star populations.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford conjecture, is a specific instance of the universal b-Teichmüller space. Furthermore, this note also defines a new topological invariant, the E1-graded E1-Hurewicz algebra, which is another way of expressing the E1-graded E1-double suspension isomorphism typically associated with the Madsen-Weiss theorem.

The goal of deep transfer learning is to leverage pre-trained deep neural networks (DNNs) on natural image datasets for downstream tasks. These pre-trained DNNs are typically used as feature extractors for various upstream tasks across diverse datasets, enabling knowledge sharing and reducing training costs. However, their transferability tends to decline as they are applied to tasks that diverge significantly in content and complexity, resulting in subpar performance. To address these challenges, this study presents a novel approach called the Quantitative Content and Form Disentangled Neural Network (QC-FDNN) method for enhancing the transferability of DNNs to downstream tasks. By using this approach, we can isolate and separately train the content and form aspects of pre-trained DNNs in downstream content-shared but form-dissimilar knowledge spaces. To accomplish this, we developed an automatic quantitative Content-Form dataset comprising multiple content-shared and form-dissimilar medical imaging datasets. We also designed a specialized Quantitative Content-Form Disentangled Network (QC-FDNet) framework consisting of three key components: a learnable Content-Form Disentangled Siamese Network (CFD-SNet), a novel contrastive content regularization (CRCR) loss, and a novel form regularization (RF) loss. CFD-SNet, consisting of two interconnected networks - the Form Network (FN) and the Disentangled Siamese Network (DSN) - is trained to extract form features that are shared across DNNs with

In various applications, a network often divides into distinct groups of nodes, 
limiting the spread of data within each subgroup. To efficiently distribute 
information, it is crucial to comprehend how data dissemination functions in 
compartments and what factors influence its effectiveness. Our study examines 
how network characteristics, such as community structure, impact data 
dissemination during simulations of targeted spreading. Our results reveal that 
increasing community strength initially decreases the reach of data, but under 
certain conditions, this reach can be boosted by strategically selecting seed 
users. These findings align with theoretical predictions and offer insights for 
designing effective marketing and advertising campaigns that can successfully 
navigate complex network barriers.

Under specific conditions from Floer theory, we derive numerical measures indicating the proximity of two Lagrangians based on their angular separation, and these measurements depend on how close those Lagrangian angles are to being perfectly aligned. Some outcomes resulting from these conditions are a definitive existence proof for holomorphic discs and a definitive removal of the Grushin component in an analytical model known as the analytical model of the Grushin pair.

The reliability of a discrete-time channel model that uses a standard method of perturbation
is numerically investigated for cases without signal amplification. We assess the distance between 
discrete nonlinear interference points and find that this distance can be employed to estimate 
the effective memory length of the communication channel.

The widespread adoption of Android devices has led to an increase in the number of Android malwares, prompting the development of advanced detection methods along with increasingly sophisticated new malware variants capable of evading detection. Problem-space evasion attacks modify an app's functionality without changing its executable code, a process that is often difficult to replicate. To explore the effectiveness of such attacks, this research focuses on the most common type - those targeting apps with malicious data theft features. It also introduces a novel technique called de-obfuscation to reverse an app's obfuscation tools' effects and apply it to a success-oriented learning goal. Additionally, a novel app reverse-engineering tool known as AppInspector has been created to analyze an app's original application structure. The new technique along with AppInspector has been incorporated into existing automated testing pipelines for efficient app detection. Utilizing the most up-to-date version of the Google Play's top free and paid apps as well as the most popular malicious Android apps, this research has examined the most widely used Android malware families discovered to date. The findings indicate that our de-obfuscation method combined with the novel testing goal effectively outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques by 10% in detecting Android malware family variations.

Service-oriented computing has been extensively employed in software development, particularly with the concept of reusing services. Although service reuse is a core principle, the traditional understanding of a service as software functionality has been limited. It's clear that any entity capable of interaction can be integrated into the service-oriented paradigm, which necessitates software interaction models that support diverse communication types. Currently, existing interaction models are confined to web services, restricting the scope of the service-oriented paradigm to traditional web protocols only. To address this limitation, this study introduces the concept of a protocol protocol abstraction point (PPAP), enabling software interaction models to accommodate various protocols through the integration of a protocol protocol adapter (PPA). It outlines the conceptual foundation of PPAPs, along with corresponding formal formalizations, and subsequently introduces a universal universal PPAP, el universal universal protocol protocol adapter (EUPAP), designed to facilitate software interaction irrespective of the protocol employed. Ultimately, a proof-of-concept implementation of EUPAP is demonstrated, along with examination of its feasibility in practical settings.

Recent experimental observations supporting the particle-hole symmetric Pfaffian topological order are challenged by thermal Hall conductivity data, which are incompatible with this model due to its predicted properties. We propose an alternative model, the chiral topological order, which not only explains the thermal Hall conductivity but also accurately accounts for other experimental findings. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the thermal Hall effect can serve as a diagnostic tool to distinguish between chiral and particle-hole symmetric topological orders.

Our analysis indicates that the singularities harbored within Thakurta black holes are likely to occur under highly specific, localized conditions within the universe's gravitational environment. Thakurta black holes comprise a subset of more general loomis-painleve-gulliksen (LPG) metrics developed in an earlier work. Thakurta metrics are distinguished by the presence of two independent physical parameters that remain constant throughout the entire spacetime surrounding each black hole. In contrast, the LPG metrics possess four such parameters, two of which are unrelated to physical characteristics and merely reflect coordinate transformations. By assigning variable values to the independent LPG metric parameters that can influence light propagation, a broader set of black hole metrics emerges. These new metrics possess four independent parameters all with direct physical significance. Under these conditions, the LPG metrics are believed to represent a more comprehensive framework that encompasses all static black holes associated with string theory, both in two and four dimensions.

The presence of pressure bumps in a protoplanetary disk's gas can significantly affect the growth of planetary cores through gravitational instability or gaps, potentially leading to the formation of planetoids and ultimately planet formation. Our research focuses on how these pressure bumps influence planet core growth over time scales and dust accumulation in rings and valleys within gravitationally unstable discs. Our analysis of gravitational ring and valley systems shows that planet core growth is most efficient at the avian regions of these valleys, particularly near the inner boundaries. Our simulations reveal that under specific conditions, core growth can occur at lower mass rates and over shorter distances. Our simulations suggest that these valleys can accumulate sufficient solid materials to form planetoids and gas giants, but require extended time spans and radial distances. Furthermore, we find that at larger radial distances, gravitational instability may lead to disk fragmentation and the formation of planetesimals, possibly explaining the observed super-Earth mass at radial separations. Our findings also indicate that gravitational ring structures can form within thin, viscous disks, but require substantial radial distances and core masses to produce detectable signals.

This work investigates the fundamental trade-off between the number of model parameters and the ability to generalize in the presence of computational constraints. We establish that the theoretical minimum number of parameters for an exact solution to complex prediction tasks scales exponentially with the input dimension. Building on this insight, we propose a range of approximate solutions with significantly fewer model parameters, adequate to capture complex patterns with minimal error. We analyze these solutions across three distinct settings: neurons with complex activation functions, two widely used deep learning architectures, and finite element methods in computational mechanics. We establish that the actual performance of these approximate models often surpasses theoretical error bounds in terms of prediction accuracy.

The problem of translating the Fourier restriction phenomenon from real vector spaces to countable, discrete groups has been explored. Specifically, a constraint on the size and algebraic structure of a group G yields the existence of a Bohr set within the sum of the images of a subset A⊆G, given that G/pG has nontrivial structure for all primes p. Moreover, if A has a particular property, a certain growth condition on its size enables the identification of such Bohr sets within R(A), particularly within abelian G where p has prime index in G and when g<p/2, the inequality |A|>p^(s-1)+p^(s-2) holds for each prime g not dividing |G|. The research presented has further implications for the growth within nilpotent groups within the work of Bourgain. Specifically, a known estimate for non-abelian free groups is shown to be essentially tight.

This study addresses the dynamic routing problem for ridepooling, where service quality is determined by trip duration and customer effort due to vehicle deviations. To optimize this balance, we seek to minimize detours while maintaining service above a specified threshold. Due to computational limitations of existing solutions, we developed two approximations: one based on the epsilon-optimal approach and another leveraging load equality. We then incorporated these approxations into a real-time algorithm and evaluated it on standard test cases. Compared to exact solutions, it demonstrated an average relative error of less than 1% for pooling levels, achieving improvements of up to a 50% reduction in travel time.

This study explores multi-modal representation learning within the context of E-commerce. We introduce a novel multi-modal representation learning pipeline capable of handling complex modalities like images and texts that pose distinct processing challenges such as sparsity, unstructuredness, and multivariability. Our pipeline addresses these obstacles through a structured multi-stage process, where each stage utilizes specialized models to process specific modalities. We combine the processed modalities using an attention mechanism to create a unified latent space. We assess the efficacy of our proposed pipeline using three key applications: product recommendation, search and ranking, and relevant product retrieval. Utilizing a large-scale Taobao dataset comprising over 100 million products across various product categories, our experimental results demonstrate that the learned representations achieve superior performance across all three applications.

A significant function in deep learning for analyzing brain scans is Deep InfoMax (DIM).
This technique maximizes the extraction of inherent patterns in deep networks for brain imaging.
Although DIM is a prominent approach, it lacks a thorough understanding and a deep comparison with traditional supervised methods.
In this study, a high-level description and analysis of DIM are presented for multiple brain imaging tasks, and its performance is compared to a standard supervised technique.
A technical breakdown of the DIM model and associated training objectives is provided, and its performance on various modalities and tasks is tested through extensive validation experiments.
The results demonstrate that DIM can achieve competitive performance, and a method to integrate standard supervised training and DIM pre-training is discovered.
Through combining both techniques, a significant improvement in model efficiency and performance is observed, and results demonstrate that adding pre-training can enhance model performance, and notable results on multiclass classification of Alzheimer's disease are presented.

Text classification using a bag-of-words approach is an automated system that assesses the relevance of individual words within a text without considering their sequence or arrangement.  A novel method, the influence score (I-score), was developed to identify and eliminate superfluous features by measuring each word's predictive power based on its unique contribution to the text's classification.  A score between 0 and 1 is assigned to each word, reflecting its likelihood of appearing in a specific class.  On the CIFAR-10 dataset using bag-of-words features, the I-score outperformed traditional filtering techniques such as feature selection and filter-based feature evaluation, achieving improved accuracy and faster feature processing times.  In the more complex ImageNet dataset, the I-score surpassed the DenseNet model with bag-of-words features achieving 66.6% accuracy compared to the DenseNet's 65.7% accuracy, and also outperformed deep learning approaches like GoogLeNet on concepts such as text ambiguity and domain shift resistance.  A public repository showcasing various implementations of the I-score method across diverse applications has been made available.

We investigate the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model that has two directions of orbital motion aligned with a magnetic field, employing a renormalization group technique. By examining the system in the absence of magnetic order, we find that the effective spin-orbit coupling constant increases proportionally to the electron interaction strength. As interactions intensify beyond a specific threshold, spin splitting ratios become significantly larger than the bare spin-orbit coupling constant, potentially leading to new spin phenomena associated with interacting electrons. Additionally, we discover that when an orbital imbalance is initially present, the system exhibits strong coupling between orbital and spin degrees of freedom due to spin-orbit interaction, resulting in the emergence of magnetic phases dependent on orbital polarization and, under specific conditions, a topological surface state arises.

A mysterious dark sector interacting with standard model particles holds potential for both astrophysical discoveries and fundamental physics insights. The proposed setup, which connects dark matter annihilation to lepton universality violation in the weak interaction, introduces an anomaly that influences the process. This particular model generates the required dark matter abundance through this specific mechanism, allowing for an examination of its implications at the Large Hadron Collider. Furthermore, due to the limited lifespan of mediators, it becomes possible to observe their decays into dark matter particles, making this model particularly relevant for early universe dynamics as it becomes less relevant over time, thus, being a strong candidate for understanding universe formation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized medical diagnostics through advanced deep learning models, which have significantly improved cancer detection rates. However, their efficacy is often compromised when encountering diverse patient populations due to biases introduced during training. Consequently, accurately predicting AI-based medical devices' performance under varying conditions becomes crucial. Existing methods, including algorithmic fairness and causal inference, have limitations in addressing real-world biases, which are typically unknown and data-driven. This study introduces a novel framework, TEDA, which models and predicts test performance biases under real-world distribution changes by leveraging a variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture. Through simulations and evaluations on public health datasets, TEDA demonstrated superior capability in estimating performance biases compared to other established methods.

High-fidelity simulations of complete DNA and RNA molecules are capable of exploring a broad range of conformations, including dynamic movements of base pairs and the reorganization of minor grooves, by using a subset of molecular mechanics. Contrary to widely accepted views, our research indicates that an automated method can be used to determine the boundaries of the stable conformations of these molecules. The study introduces a new approach that combines existing techniques to construct a dynamic simulation framework, which is based on the electronic and force-field method, and applies it to a single-stranded DNA oligomer to evaluate its stable conformations. The findings of this study have the potential to inform a new approach to designing small molecules, including drugs, that interact with nucleic acids.

The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) is a powerful lossless compression algorithm that achieves excellent compression rates by utilizing arithmetic coding without fractional parts. In this research, we present theoretical findings regarding a table-based ANS encoder known as the tabled ANS (tANS) encoder. We specifically analyze the redundancy incurred by this tANS encoder using different initialization methods, one proposed by Duda and another developed by us. We demonstrate that the tANS encoder using Duda's precise initialization method results in a redundancy of O(ω/log(ω)) where ω represents the current ANS state, plus a non-negative constant. We also show that this redundancy is achieved with at most O(ω) operations. We further establish that tANS redundancy grows at most linearly with time. We propose an even lower bounded redundancy growth at some constant times t0. We verify that using data compression's standard metrics, the tANS encoder results in suboptimal compressor redundancy. We show that tANS redundancy is non-optimal by at least a non-zero constant for n ≥ n0 where n represents the input length, n0 being a non-negative constant. We counter potential objections to our results by illustrating that simple renormalization methods fail to reduce tANS redundancy below optimality threshold, resulting in redundancy growth at least at constant 1/4.

The dielectric characteristics of liquid solutions are heavily influenced by ion interactions, especially within high concentration regimes. Computational simulations have been conducted using spherical molecules to model electrolytes. These simulations were analyzed using theoretical frameworks including mean spherical approximation and dielectric continuum theory. Comparing results from various models to Monte Carlo simulation outcomes revealed the dielectric continuum theory to be accurate in the moderate concentration range but falls short in the high concentration regime. Simulated dielectric responses were further compared to experimental data, confirming their alignment.

In our research, we propose the existence of a spectrum consisting of heavyantiheavy bound states. These bound states, or hadronic molecules, can be categorized according to quantum numbers such as angular momentum and parity. Certain molecules like the $DD^*$, $D^*_S D_S^*$, $D^*_SS$, $\Psi_d D^*$, $D^*_S D^*_S$, $D^*_D D^*_D$, $D^*_L D^*_L$, $D^*_A D^*_A$, $D^*_I D^*_I$, $D^*_J D^*_J$, $D^*_O D^*_O$, $D^*_P D^*_P$, $D^*_K D^*_K$, $D^*_N D^*_N$, $D^*_R D^*_R$, $D^*_U D^*_U$, $D^*_V D^*_V$, $D^*_W D^*_W$, $D^*Y D^*Y$, $D^*K_D^*$, $D^*K_D^*$, $D^*_N D^*_N$, $D^*_R D^*_R$, $D^*_U D^*_U$, $D^*_V D^*_V$, $D^*_W D^*_W$, $D^*_Y D^

Research on military drones is growing rapidly, with numerous studies being published. 
However, to date, a significant knowledge gap exists, as the research levels of military drones have not been analyzed comprehensively from a systematic and scientific perspective.
To bridge this gap, our study employs bibliometric analysis to examine the current state of military drone research.
Using the Web of Science database and the Bibliometrix tool, we examined nearly 5,900 peer-reviewed papers over the past 30 years.
The findings of our analysis reveal that the years 2019 and 2020 witnessed a surge in military drone drone studies.
Our study identifies the primary researchers and institutions driving military drone studies, and pinpoints the most influential journals and countries in this field.
Further, our results outline the most prolific journals and countries in military drone studies and identify emerging research areas and trends.

This study employs Markov-Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis to reconstruct the cosmic web's density fluctuations from the shapes of Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions and the baryon acoustic oscillation peak positions. The sample consists of 1D and 2D power spectra derived from four quasamples at redshifts of 2.35 and 2.65 from the SDSS-III BOSS survey. The parameters of the Chudomov model are used to fit the sample and constrain key cosmological parameters. The sample's constraints on the Hubble constant, $\Omega_{m}$, and the equation-of-state of dark energy, $w$, are compared to those from traditional cosmological observations. The sample's Hubble tension constraint of $1\sigma$ is notably tighter than that from the cosmic microwave background (CMB) data. The sample's $w$ parameter is consistent with a cosmological model with no interaction between dark energy and dark energy.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where a beam of particles undergoes an unconventional manipulation, swapping its horizontal and longitudinal beam patterns at the A0 Photoinjector. The new experimental setup, featuring a specially designed deflector accompanied by curved beamsplitting components, has enabled the first observation of a distinct phase shift between the particle beam's trajectory and its temporal distribution.

Pedestrian tracking technology, encompassing systems like surveillance, self-driving vehicles, and augmented reality, heavily relies on accurate trajectory prediction. A lack of appropriate evaluation metrics and annotated public datasets, however, presents a significant challenge to advancing the accuracy of pedestrian tracking. This study presents a novel and comprehensive public dataset called CHASE-DB, which encompasses a total of 14,948 video clips featuring more than 1.8 million individuals in various social situations that significantly influence their movement. A significant highlight of the CHASE-DB is the video's diversity in social interactions and movement patterns, offering a more realistic understanding of the complexities involved in tracking humans. With well-annotated data and innovative algorithms, researchers can significantly benefit from using the CHASE-DB to improve object tracking. A baseline model has also been developed using the latest object tracking techniques to serve as a starting point for future advancements.

Over the past two decades, various theoretical models have been introduced to analyze the complexity of neural networks, with a particular focus on understanding the relationship between computational capacity and network structure. This work delves into the dynamics of complexity within a specific type of neural network, specifically a recurrent auto-associative network, in response to different training methods. It investigates how the two primary forms of Hebbian learning - purely associative and associative-hetero associative - affect complexity evolution, as evidenced by analysis of auto-associative networks trained under these conditions. Through this exploration, it becomes evident that both trained and untrained sections of the network contribute to complexity when using purely associative Hebbian training, while in hetero-associative training, only the learned segment adds to complexity. Furthermore, it has been observed that in hetero-associative training, the untrained segments experience a reduction in complexity due to a destructive interference mechanism inherent to the associated associative process. These results offer valuable insights into how computational models can be designed to resist degradation over time.

This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for facilitating communication between humans and a swarm of robots. Our solution involves utilizing a hand gesture recognition system powered by a CNN-FCN architecture, trained on the widely-used YouTube dataset. Our experiment involved releasing a swarm of 20 robots in a controlled environment and observing their behavior in response to distinct hand gestures. We successfully demonstrated that our system can reliably translate hand gestures into actionable instructions for a swarm of robots. Our research also includes an in-depth analysis of the accuracy and latency of the hand gesture recognition system.

The study presents findings on using convolutional neural networks and transfer learning for automatically categorizing white blood cells from image data. An image dataset of ~5000 white blood cell images is shared. Although a fully customized CNN is typically most effective for a specific task, it requires substantial labeled data. As an alternative, this research explored using a pre-trained, general-purpose CNN developed by Facebook AI for a variety of image classification tasks. Our results using a simplified, reduced dataset indicate that even this general-purpose CNN achieved a 65% accuracy rate, demonstrating a notable performance in a specialized medical application despite being designed for a broad range of image tasks by Facebook AI.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a carefully selected auxiliary system, known as the counterdiabatic Hamiltonian, to streamline the process. Unfortunately, for complex systems like many-body Hamiltonians applied to initial coherent states, there is no one-size-fits-all solution to this Hamiltonian. In response, we have developed a technique for generating an approximate counterdiabatic Hamiltonian tailored to complex many-body systems and initial coherent states. We have successfully tested our technique by facilitating the rapid transformation of a Bose-Einstein condensate's ground state into a $\pi$-shifted version, even in the presence of strong environmental interference. Our findings highlight the potential of this method for achieving effective quantum state manipulation in fast transformations, especially in systems prone to dephasing.

Significant amounts of data are generated through image grayscale, processing, and analysis, and techniques within this field have the potential to resolve critical problems, such as those encountered in medical imaging, satellite communication, and satellite imaging. Nevertheless, real-world images often suffer from various types of degradation due to poor processing, environmental factors, and other uncontrollable variables. In order to restore these images, under-supervised image processing methods are applied, and a proposed new approach aims to improve existing techniques by learning image-to-image transformations in a self-supervised manner. In this context, we introduce an innovative framework, SS2ITL, based on image similarity learning through self-supervision, and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in restoring images, and we discuss the potential of incorporating domain transformation learning and adaptation within this framework.

This article presents an innovative approach to expressing differentiable complex-valued functions as a combination of exponentials with associated coefficients that are relatively small in magnitude. By doing so, it enables the construction of compact, structure-preserving, high-order accurate, and efficient methods for solving time-dependent problems that involve spatial derivatives. These issues arise in various scientific domains such as physics, mechanics, and other engineering fields. The proposed technique leverages the properties of the Fourier transform to define an iterative algorithm for determining coefficients of the exponential sum approximation. A detailed analysis of the associated approximation and propagation errors is provided, along with numerical examples to illustrate the method's application and validate the theoretical findings.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, such that it meets the conditions set by Alexandrov for an upper curvature bound, we demonstrate that an almost conformal harmonic map from a surface to the pair (S, d) results in a branched covering. Consequently, if (S, d) is topologically equivalent to the two-dimensional sphere S^2, it then becomes conformally equivalent to S^2.

We've created a state-of-the-art simulation of the linear Breit-Wheeler process using advanced gamma-source technology and 3D laser plasma acceleration to achieve high photon densities in a precise target area. By combining the photons from the gamma source with an extremely powerful laser beam, we've concentrated the potential for the collision that generates electron-positron pairs at specific locations. Furthermore, our approach allows us to control and replicate the conditions in which this process takes place, thereby enabling future high-energy physics experiments at the linear energy threshold. Our comprehensive report outlines and validates the entire process, examining the generation of the photon source, the characteristics of the resulting photons, and the characteristics of the photons within the ultra-intense laser focus.

A recent analysis of LHC data has significantly narrowed down the possible range for the Two Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM) parameter space. With the latest data from Run 2, the allowed range with 95% confidence is 11 times smaller than before, notably, the previously uncertain type-2 2HDM is no longer excluded. Prior to the analysis, the allowed range was well described by a Minimal Standard Higgs Model and a Minimal Darkness Higgs Model. Future colliders will need to precisely determine the 2HDM CP properties to fill the gap in understanding how the 125 GeV scalar particle interacts. With the possibility of the LHC's third run soon, the allowed range will be further refined and well understood with future colliders like ILC, CLIC, FCC-ee, and CEPC.

We examine the RDF data exchange scenario based on relational data, characterized by a unique source and multiple targets, all conforming to the Data Model for Resource Description Framework.
